title: Marzipan fruits
subtitle: Hand-moulded marzipan shaped and painted to look like miniature fruits
excerpt: Moulded marzipan fruits are made by rolling shop-bought or home-made marzipan into small balls and shaping them by hand into strawberries, oranges, lemons, and other fruits, then painting them with food colouring diluted in a little water or spirit. No special equipment is needed: the tools are your hands and a fine paintbrush.
sourceNotes: Marzipan fruits are a European confectionery tradition with documented roots in Lubeck, Spain, and Sicily from the medieval period onwards. In the UK they became associated with Christmas and celebration boxes of assorted confectionery. The moulding and painting technique is documented in classic confectionery and cake-decoration texts.

recipe.batchNotes: Scale up freely; 500 g marzipan gives about 50 pieces. Marzipan keeps in the fridge for 3 months before use.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Moulded and painted fruits keep in a cool, dry place in an airtight box for up to 3 weeks. They should not touch each other or the colour will transfer.

glossaryTerms.definition: Marzipan can be coloured before moulding by kneading gel food colouring into the paste, or painted after shaping using food colouring diluted in a small amount of water or clear spirit. Painting after shaping gives more control over tone: a sponged base coat followed by brush strokes of a darker shade produces the bloom and shading of real fruit better than a single solid colour.

content.text: is what lifts these from coloured lumps to convincing miniature fruits. A two-step approach works: knead a pale base colour into the marzipan before shaping, then add shading and surface detail with a brush after the shaped pieces have dried.

items.prepNote: red, yellow, green, and orange gel colours

content.text: Divide the marzipan into portions (around 10 g each) and keep each piece covered in cling film when not in use; marzipan dries out quickly. Shape each portion as follows:
Strawberry: roll into a slightly pointed oval. Roll lightly over a fine grater or tea strainer to texture the surface. Paint red when dry, add tiny dots of green for seeds.
Orange: roll into a ball. Press lightly all over against a grater to give the pitted skin texture. Paint orange. Add a tiny clove pressed into the top if available.
Lemon: roll into an oval and pinch gently at each end to give the characteristic tips. Texture the surface with a grater. Paint yellow with a brush, deepening the ends with orange.
Banana: roll into a thin curved cylinder. Pinch the ends flat and curve the piece gently. Paint yellow when dry; add brown brush strokes along the ridges.

Leave shaped pieces on baking paper at room temperature for at least 1 hour before painting so a dry skin forms. Dilute gel colours with a few drops of water to make a thin, transparent wash. Apply a base coat with a soft brush or a crumpled piece of kitchen paper for a mottled effect. Leave to dry, then add shading with a slightly darker mix brushed lightly over curves and indentations.
